item.title: Kubernetes Descheduler Guide: Pod Rebalancing and Eviction Strategy
item.description:
Overview

Kubernetes relies on kube-scheduler to evaluate cluster topology, filter eligible nodes, and assign newly created pods to optimal worker nodes. However, this scheduling decision is strictly a point-in-time calculation executed only when a pod enters the scheduling queue. Once a pod is bound to a node, Kubernetes never relocates it dynamically. As production clusters undergo node restarts, spot instance terminations, horizontal workload scaling, node taint adjustments, and organic traffic drift, the initial distribution degrades rapidly. item.description:

Enterprise security in cloud-native environments cannot rely solely on static container image vulnerability scanning (such as Trivy or Grype) and admission control policy enforcement (such as Kyverno or OPA/Gatekeeper). Even pods that pass every pre-deployment verification check remain vulnerable during active execution to zero-day exploits, remote code execution (RCE), unauthorized interactive shell takeovers, privilege escalation, and container escapes. Securing modern Kubernetes workloads therefore requires an active runtime defense layer capable of monitoring low-level container actions directly at the Linux kernel boundary and neutralizing threats the instant they occur.

item.title: Multus CNI: Multi-Homed Pods with Macvlan, SR-IOV, and PBR
item.description:
Overview

In standard Kubernetes networking, every Pod is provisioned with a single virtual network interface (eth0) connected to a cluster overlay network. This single-IP-per-Pod design simplifies communication across microservices by ensuring that all Pods can communicate without NAT. However, in enterprise environments running high-bandwidth storage synchronization (Ceph, NFS), real-time streaming, telecommunications workloads (VNF/CNF), or regulatory financial networks, a single interface introduces severe throughput bottlenecks and security isolation challenges.

Multus CNI is a meta-plugin that enables Kubernetes Pods to attach multiple distinct network interfaces (eth0, net1, net2, etc.)...
